clue.text: There seems to 'be nothing in the centre of this crowd.

parts.words: There seems to 'be nothing in the centre
parts.note: the setter's reading: nothing is O, a zero, and the word's middle letter is just that
the setter's reading: a three-letter word for a disorderly throng; the stray apostrophe is a flaw in the old print

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is the letter O, like a zero, and the word for a rough crowd has an O at its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A disorderly throng of people is a rough synonym for crowd.

clue.text: This singer seems to be adrift.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the high adult male voice
the surface reading suggests a boat cut loose; the setter's reading: the word also means a drift, the general sense of what is said

explanation.walkthrough: 'The tenor of his remarks' means their drift, so the singer's name seems to be 'a drift'.
explanation.definitionFit: The high natural male voice in a choir gives its name to the man who sings that part.

parts.note: the surface reading: something plainly worthwhile, not a failure
the setter's reading: a dud is a shell that fails to explode, so this is one that plainly did go off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dud' sounds like slang for a flop; in the war just past it meant a shell that failed to explode, and a shell that exploded showed it was not one.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploded shell has visibly gone off, the very opposite of a dud that lies inert.

parts.note: the setter's reading: people who employ something in the old sense, that is, make use of it
the surface reading suggests crooked bosses; the setter's reading: the word's letters rearrange to a word for tricks or deceptions

explanation.walkthrough: To employ is also to use, and USERS rearranges to RUSES, which are frauds; the puzzle plays this letter game more than once.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who make use of a thing are, in the older sense of the verb, employing it.

clue.text: Your work may be hung up here.

definitions.text: Your work may be hung up here

parts.words: Your work may be hung up
parts.note: the surface reading: work delayed or put on a hook
the setter's reading: the annual Paris art exhibition where accepted paintings were hung

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hung up' suggests delay; the work is a painting, hung on the walls of the Paris exhibition.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Paris exhibition hung artists' accepted canvases, and the word also names any gallery room.

clue.text: You may take hand in this.

definitions.text: You may take hand in this

parts.note: the surface reading: join in, take a hand in something
the setter's reading: the soft leather gloves are made of, so your hand goes inside it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a hand in' sounds like joining in; the hand literally goes into a glove of this soft leather.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft napped leather, much used for gloves, is the material a hand is put into.

parts.note: the surface reading: people getting into bed
the setter's reading: sheets of paper, with copying paper laid between them in a typewriter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheets' suggests bedding; the sheets are paper, and the inked copying paper sits between them to make a duplicate.
explanation.definitionFit: Inked copying paper is placed between two sheets so that typing on the top one prints on the lower.

clue.text: There might be garage space, it seems, in this little house.

parts.words: There might be garage space, it seems,
parts.note: the setter's reading: the word appears to say there is a taxi inside, which would need a garage
the setter's reading: a small simple dwelling, such as a hut or cottage

explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as CAB IN: a cab is in it, so it seems to have garage space.
explanation.definitionFit: A small simple dwelling, such as a hut in the woods, is a little house.

definitions.note: the clue gives no definition at all: early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation is the setter saying outright that the preceding words are to be rearranged

parts.note: the seven letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: With no definition, the solver looks for the only word these letters make, and the crossing letters confirm it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the train of attendants who accompany an important person.

clue.text: This is a defence with the Senior Service on, the 38 flanks.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a V-shaped earthwork, like the one stormed at Sebastopol in the Crimean War

parts.words: with the Senior Service on, the 38 flanks
parts.note: the setter's reading: the Senior Service is the Royal Navy, abbreviated RN, and its letters stand on the word's two flanks

explanation.walkthrough: RN, the Royal Navy, is the 'Senior Service'; R and N stand at either end of REDAN. The '38' in the print does not account for the middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A redan is a fieldwork of two walls meeting in a point toward the enemy, a military fortification.

clue.text: Not a dish, though often on the menu.

definitions.text: Not a dish, though often on the menu

parts.note: the surface reading: something listed among the food yet not food itself
the setter's reading: the French phrase meaning 'in the style of', as in a dish described 'à la mode'

explanation.walkthrough: Menus describe dishes as 'à la something', so the phrase appears constantly without being a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase meaning 'in the manner of' crops up on menus to describe how food is prepared.

parts.note: the surface reading: the here and now; the setter's reading: the word for this moment
the setter's reading: the word for this spot, run together with the first to make a word meaning no place at all

explanation.walkthrough: Join NOW to HERE and the result, ironically, means no place at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The two words for this moment and this spot, written solid, become a word for nonexistent location.

parts.note: the surface reading: something with a strict cap
the setter's reading: there are just two kinds, male and female

explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe is a speck on the old print. The joke is that the category famously comes in only two varieties.
explanation.definitionFit: Gender in the biological sense is divided into male and female, so it has just two forms.

parts.note: the surface reading: some disputed issue
the setter's reading: the idiom 'a ___ of contention', a point fought over like a dog's prize

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'bone of contention' comes from two dogs fighting over one bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Completing the idiom gives the thing that two dogs, or two parties, quarrel over.

clue.text: You may feel this if successful.
These attacks supply their own reinforcement.

definitions.text: These attacks supply their own reinforcement

parts.note: the setter's reading: sudden assaults or incursions
the surface reading sounds like troops bringing reserves; the setter means the word holds within it a word for help

explanation.walkthrough: Reinforcement means help, and RAIDS carries AIDS inside its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden short assaults by a force, often at night, are the attacks named.

clue.text: Three attempts is the proverbial allowance don't do it at once.

definitions.text: Three attempts is the proverbial allowance don't do it at once

parts.words: Three attempts is the proverbial allowance
parts.note: the setter's reading: the proverb 'if at first you don't ___, try, try, try again'
the setter's reading: the proverb allows for failing the first time, which is not managing it at once

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'If at first you don't succeed, try, try, try again': three tries are allowed for not doing it first time.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve what you attempt is exactly what the proverb says you may fail to do at first.

clue.text: This means the same as its own anagram.

definitions.text: This means the same as its own anagram

parts.note: the setter's reading: an old word for yes
the setter's reading: rearrange its three letters and you get the other old word for yes, used in Parliament's votes

explanation.walkthrough: YEA and AYE are both archaic forms of yes, and each is the other's letters reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: The old affirmative is a synonym of its own rearrangement, the voting cry heard in the Commons.

clue.text: This is where you draw the line.

definitions.text: This is where you draw the line

parts.words: This is where you draw the line
parts.note: the surface reading: the idiom for the limit of what you will tolerate
the setter's reading: literally ruling a straight pencil line along a measuring edge

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means setting a limit; the setter means the straight edge a pencil runs along.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight-edged measuring strip is the tool along which you literally draw lines.

clue.text: The clue should make you do this.

definitions.text: The clue should make you do this

parts.note: the surface reading: the setter speaking about this very puzzle
the setter's reading: respond, as a stimulus provokes a response

explanation.walkthrough: The setter steps out of the puzzle: a clue is a prompt, and a prompt is meant to get a response.
explanation.definitionFit: To respond to a stimulus is what any prompt or cue is meant to make you do.

parts.note: the surface reading: the answer to this clue
the setter's reading: a chemical solution, the strong alkaline liquid used in soap-making

explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' sounds like the crossword answer; it is also a liquid mixture, and this one is caustic.
explanation.definitionFit: Lye is a strongly alkaline liquid leached from wood ash, used for washing and soap-making.

clue.text: This is not to be taken seriously
This is better to drive than to ride.

definitions.text: This is better to drive than to ride

parts.note: the setter's reading: a threaded fastener you drive into wood
the setter's reading: the same word is old slang for a broken-down horse, no pleasure to ride

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' and 'ride' suggest a horse or car; a screw is driven by a screwdriver, and 'screw' was also slang for a worn-out nag.
explanation.definitionFit: A threaded metal fastener is driven home, while the same word for a decrepit horse makes a poor mount.

clue.text: You may get a bit of a laugh out of this one.

parts.note: the surface reading: the setter warning of a contradiction
the setter's reading: the tiered seating at a sports ground, named by the word for being upright

explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is that spectators sit in a stand, though the word means to be on your feet.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised tier of seating at a racecourse or ground carries the name of the upright position.

indicators.note: 'may be' says the next word could become something else, so its letters can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; the hyphen before it is a flaw in the old print

explanation.surface: A disfiguring mark that can be painful, even cruel, to bear.
explanation.definitionFit: An open sore on the skin or a membrane is a disfigurement, a kind of blemish.

definitions.note: the clue gives no definition at all: early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation is the setter saying outright that the preceding words are to be rearranged

parts.note: the seven letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: With no definition, the solver looks for the only word these letters make, and the crossing letters confirm it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old literary term for clothing or apparel.

clue.text: "He at scars that never felt a wound."

definitions.text: "He at scars that never felt a wound."

parts.note: the setter's reading: a word is missing after 'He', and it is the answer
the surface reading: Romeo's line in Romeo and Juliet about Mercutio, who mocks love because he has never been in love

explanation.walkthrough: The full line from Romeo and Juliet is 'He jests at scars that never felt a wound'; the answer is the word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb, meaning makes fun of, completes Shakespeare's line about mocking pain you have never known.

clue.text: This craft is made of rather than for salt water.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a small light boat paddled by hand

parts.words: of rather than for salt water
parts.note: the surface reading suggests a seagoing vessel; the setter means the boat's name is built from the letters of a word for the sea

explanation.walkthrough: Salt water is the OCEAN, and CANOE uses exactly those five letters, so the craft is made of it rather than built for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A light narrow boat paddled by hand is a small craft in the nautical sense.

parts.note: the setter's reading: one word of a fixed phrase
the surface reading: a retort; the setter's reading: the phrase for returning blow for blow, 'tit for ___'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tit for tat' means paying back like with like, a retaliation, and the answer is its last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The closing word of the stock phrase for retaliation in kind is one piece of that retort.

parts.note: the setter's reading: to destroy can be to eat, as rust or acid eats metal
the setter's reading: drop the last letter of the word and the four left rearrange into that verb

explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle plays this letter trick several times (CANOE and ocean, ULCER and cruel): most of TEASE is TEAS, which rearranges to EATS, meaning destroys.
explanation.definitionFit: To tease is to pester or make fun of someone, and the clue is a game with its own letters rather than a definition.

indicators.note: backward tells you to read the word from its last letter to its first

parts.note: to break sharply in two is to snap

explanation.surface: A footballer who crosses the ball forward and then breaks back down the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' marks the word as read normally for the definition, against 'backward' for the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge that crosses a river is said to bridge it, a synonym of crosses in the sense of stretching over.

clue.text: The bear would not have been reduced to it if he had kept his head.

indicators.text: if he had kept his head
indicators.note: the bear lost his head, so the creature's name is used without its opening letter

parts.note: Bruin is the traditional storybook name for a bear

explanation.surface: A bear brought low who would have fared better had he kept a cool head.
explanation.walkthrough: Bruin is the folk-tale name for a bear; take off his head and he is RUIN, the state he was reduced to.
explanation.definitionFit: To be reduced to ruin is to be brought to utter collapse, so the noun is what the bear came to.

parts.note: the surface reading: things judged dull and plodding
the setter's reading: literally to do with going on foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' usually means dull, but literally means on foot, and walking styles are just that.
explanation.definitionFit: Manners of walking or running, such as the trot or amble, are all movements made on foot.

clue.text: A form, in the plural, of 3 down.

definitions.text: A form, in the plural, of 3 down

parts.note: the setter's reading: a kind or type of the thing in 3 down
the setter's reading: a tailor's pressing iron is called a goose, from its curved handle, and more than one take an irregular plural

explanation.walkthrough: 3 down is IRON; a tailor's smoothing iron is called a goose, and its plural is GEESE, not gooses.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailors' heavy pressing irons, called gooses or geese for their neck-like handles, are one sort of iron.

clue.text: Used to be a farthing a-piece.

definitions.text: Used to be a farthing a-piece

parts.note: the surface reading: some bygone bargain
the setter's reading: cheap candles made by dipping a rush or wick in tallow, sold for a farthing, a quarter of an old penny

explanation.walkthrough: A farthing was the smallest British coin, a quarter of a penny; tallow candles made by dipping were the cheapest light.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallow candles made by repeatedly plunging a wick into melted fat were sold for the smallest coin.

clue.text: This suggests the abbreviated person with which it begins.

definitions.text: This suggests the abbreviated person with which it begins

parts.note: the setter's reading: an adjective for refined, polite manners

parts.words: the abbreviated person with which it begins
parts.note: the setter's reading: a short word for a well-bred man opens the answer, and the answer describes his manners

explanation.walkthrough: GENT is the shortened form of gentleman, and GENTEEL starts with it and describes gentlemanly refinement.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means polite and refined in the manner of the upper classes.

parts.note: the surface reading: for one single aim, or something to do with the flatfish
the setter's reading: for wiping the soles of shoes at a door

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole' looks like 'only' or the fish; it is the underside of a shoe, which you wipe on a doormat.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat exists for cleaning the undersides of footwear before you step inside.

parts.note: the surface reading: our superiors in rank
the setter's reading: betters are people who bet, so what they did was gamble

explanation.walkthrough: 'Betters' looks like social superiors; read it as people who bet.
explanation.definitionFit: Staking money on an outcome is the past act of anyone who places bets.

clue.text: The wee lamb may come to this.

definitions.text: The wee lamb may come to this

indicators.note: 'may come to' says a word can be turned into something else, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three letters to rearrange, taken as written
no letters: part of the whole-clue definition, since a lamb grows up into the answer

explanation.surface: A tiny lamb will in time grow into a grown sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, since a female lamb grows into a ewe, and the word 'wee' itself rearranges into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A female lamb matures into the adult female sheep, so that is what it may become.

clue.text: Decidedly a bit of a poet.

definitions.text: Decidedly a bit of a poet

indicators.note: only a bit is wanted, so the word that follows loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written, the four letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone who is unmistakably something of a versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe was decidedly a poet, and his name is three-quarters of the word POET.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author of The Raven was a celebrated verse writer as well as a storyteller.

parts.note: the surface reading: pistols with a rotating chamber
the setter's reading: bodies that revolve, orbiting their planets; the apostrophe is a flaw in the old print

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolvers' suggests handguns; the setter means things that revolve around a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural satellites circle their planets endlessly, so they are literally things that revolve.

clue.text: A contrary outcast will be repulsive here.

definitions.note: the verb means to drive away, which is what something repulsive does

indicators.note: contrary means facing the opposite way, so the word is read from its end back to its start

parts.note: a leper was shunned and driven out, so the word means a social outcast

explanation.surface: An outcast who turns awkward will only drive others further away.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive back or push away is the action of something repulsive in the literal sense.

clue.text: This diminishes with the approach of bankruptcy.

definitions.text: This diminishes with the approach of bankruptcy

parts.note: the surface reading: something that shrinks
the setter's reading: a thing of value on the balance sheet, which dwindles as a firm fails

explanation.walkthrough: A firm heading for bankruptcy sees its holdings of value shrink until debts outweigh them.
explanation.definitionFit: An item of value owned by a business is what drains away as insolvency nears.
